title: SK hynix Unveils First HBF Standard Specifications with SanDisk at FMS 2026
event_hint: SK hynix and SanDisk released the first open standard specifications for High Bandwidth Flash (HBF) via OCP, announced at FMS 2026 (Santa Clara, Aug 4-6, 2026); HBF is positioned as a new memory layer between HBM and SSDs for AI inference.
problem: AI inference is driving a surge in data volumes to process, creating simultaneous memory-bandwidth and capacity-scalability bottlenecks that existing HBM (high bandwidth, limited capacity) and SSD (high capacity, lower bandwidth) layers each only partially address.
mechanism: High Bandwidth Flash (HBF) is positioned as a new memory layer between HBM and SSDs: it leverages NAND die stacking to deliver HBM-like high-speed data transfer while significantly expanding capacity beyond what HBM provides. The standard adopts the UCIe industry-standard die-to-die interconnect so HBF can integrate across processor types (GPUs, CPUs), and it defines connection interfaces/electrical characteristics, reliability and packaging guidelines for the HBF die-stack process, and software I/O guidelines. The specification was published as an open standard through the Open Compute Project (OCP).

evidence.claim: HBF capacity specifications cover up to 512GB, based on two stack configurations (8-high and 16-high NAND dies).
evidence.condition: Announced standard specification (8-high / 16-high NAND die stacks); not a measured shipping device
evidence.source_locator: Spec paragraph: 'Capacity specifications cover up to 512GB based on two stack configurations (8-high and 16-high NAND dies)'

evidence.claim: HBF bandwidth is categorized into three grades (Grade1-3), delivering scalable performance from approximately 0.4TB/s to 3.0TB/s.
evidence.condition: Announced standard specification across Grade1~3; spec target, not an independent measured result
evidence.source_locator: Spec paragraph: 'Bandwidth is categorized into three grades (Grade1~3), delivering scalable performance from approximately 0.4TB/s to 3.0TB/s'

evidence.claim: HBF adopts the UCIe industry-standard interconnect, laying the groundwork to integrate HBF across different processor types including GPUs and CPUs.
evidence.condition: Standard specification; processor-portability is a stated design intent
evidence.source_locator: Interconnect paragraph: 'HBF technology adopts UCIe ... to flexibly integrate ... across different processor types, including GPUs and CPUs'

evidence.claim: HBF is positioned as a new memory layer between HBM and SSDs, enabling high-speed data transfer similar to HBM while significantly expanding capacity by leveraging NAND technology, targeting AI inference bandwidth and capacity bottlenecks.
evidence.condition: Vendor positioning statement; no quantitative HBM-vs-HBF comparison visible in the evidence pack
evidence.source_locator: HBF technology paragraph: 'a new memory layer between HBM and SSDs ... high-speed data transfer similar to HBM while significantly expanding capacity by leveraging NAND technology'

evidence.claim: The HBF standard was disclosed as an open standard through the Open Compute Project (OCP); the consortium launched ~February 2026 after the initial SK hynix-SanDisk standardization partnership in August 2025, with Google and Tenstorrent currently participating.
evidence.condition: Open standard via OCP; consortium status as of Aug 4, 2026 announcement
evidence.source_locator: OCP/consortium paragraphs: 'disclosed through the Open Compute Project (OCP) ... about six months after launching the consortium in February ... Google and Tenstorrent currently participating'

evaluation_context: This is a vendor product/standardization announcement (SK hynix newsroom), not an experimental or system-evaluation paper. No measured benchmarks, no real-workload results, no independent validation in the evidence. Visible quantitative specs: capacity up to 512GB (8-high/16-high NAND stacks); bandwidth ~0.4-3.0 TB/s across three grades; UCIe interconnect. Venue: FMS 2026, Santa Clara Convention Center, Aug 4-6, 2026. Standardization timeline: SK hynix-SanDisk partnership Aug 2025, consortium launch Feb 2026, spec unveiling Aug 4, 2026.
limitations: The announcement discloses standard specifications, not a mass-produced, sampled, or deployed product; per the project-context card, announced specs must be distinguished from sampling, mass production, and scale deployment, and these spec numbers should not be read as measured device capabilities. The evidence pack contains no access latency, P/E endurance, write amplification, power draw, cost/bit, or system-level / real-workload performance data. Headline comparative claims referenced in discovery (roughly 2.5x power-efficiency gain over a prior generation and ~540x capacity vs HBM) are NOT present in the visible Evidence Pack and are therefore not recorded as facts. No independent third-party validation; the source is a vendor newsroom/marketing release.
project_relevance: HBF directly addresses the storage-media topic's question of whether a new non-volatile medium can shift the AI memory hierarchy boundary: it is an OCP open standard for a NAND-stacked, UCIe-interfaced layer sitting between HBM and SSDs, with concrete capacity (up to 512GB) and bandwidth (0.4-3.0 TB/s) specs. It is relevant to judging whether media innovation is moving from device metrics toward system usability, but the visible evidence only reaches the announced-standard stage, not measured system value. For the project, the open-standard + UCIe + multi-vendor-consortium framing (SK hynix, SanDisk, Google, Tenstorrent) is a deployment-ecosystem signal worth tracking, while power, endurance, latency, cost, and a clear mass-production timeline remain the gating unknowns. (Project inference, separate from source facts.)
